Good morning. Before we open the case, one house rule. In this room, the person who asks the sharpest question learns more than the person who gives the longest answer, so I want questions early and I want them specific. If a number in the exhibit does not make sense to you, say so. The odds are that thirty other people are quiet for exactly the same reason. And when you push on something, push on the premise, not on the person. I would want to probe the assumption behind exhibit four is a serious question. The author is wrong is a comment, and comments end conversations. One more thing. If you need clarification, ask for it in the first ten minutes, not in the last five. That is everything. Let us open the case.

Can I give you the note from the mock interview? Your content was strong. The pricing story landed. But when I asked you where the limits of your model are, you answered in two seconds, and that speed reads as defensive, not confident. Here is what a senior candidate does instead. First, buy yourself the room. That is an important question. Before I answer directly, let me give you some context. Then, and this is the part almost nobody does, ask something back. Could I ask what kind of limit you have in mind, technical or commercial? You are not stalling. You are making sure you answer the question they actually asked, and you sound like a peer instead of a candidate. Try it again on Thursday. Same question, and take four seconds before you speak.

First, the interviewer asks a wide and difficult question. Then the candidate buys the room with a short redirect line. After that, he asks an indirect question to find out what the interviewer really means. Next, he answers the narrower question with one example. Finally, he checks that the answer landed with a tag question.
